idiom_name: Scala 3 enum cases (or sealed trait) + match interpreter
implementation_notes: Scala 3 `enum` cases (or a sealed trait with case classes) form the closed algebra and `match` is checked for exhaustiveness, so one interpreter is one match and a new operation breaks every interpreter at compile time; programs are immutable values with structural equality, which is why tagless-final is the usual alternative only when no data structure is wanted. Depth is the caveat: match-based interpreters need tail-recursive shapes, `cats.Eval` or an explicit stack for deep programs.
code_sketch:
enum Op:
  case Get(key: String)
  case Put(key: String, value: Int)

def run(op: Op, store: Store): Int = op match
  case Op.Get(k)    => store.read(k)
  case Op.Put(k, v) => store.write(k, v)
pitfalls: Exhaustiveness holds only for enums/sealed hierarchies in one compilation unit; extending a trait across files or adding `@unchecked` defeats it.
Pattern matching on generic case classes erases type parameters (unchecked warnings) - carry type tags where the operation needs them.
Deeply recursive interpreters overflow the stack; use Cats' Eval/trampolining or make the recursion iterative.

variants.name: Cats Free monad with FunctionK interpreters
variants.idiom_name: cats.free.Free + liftF smart constructors + FunctionK natural transformation
variants.implementation_notes: `Free[Op, A]` reifies the program as a recursive structure, `liftF` builds smart constructors, and an interpreter is a `FunctionK[Op, M]` natural transformation folded with `foldMap` into `Id`, `IO` or `Future` - a production interpreter performs the effects and an in-memory one can be built on State. `foldMap` is stack-safe by trampolining, which is the strongest reason to pay the encoding cost for long-running programs. Use it when the same program must run in several monads or stack safety is required; otherwise the plain ADT variant is simpler.
variants.code_sketch:
sealed trait OpA[A]
case class Get(key: String) extends OpA[Option[Int]]
case class Put(key: String, v: Int) extends OpA[Unit]

type Op[A] = Free[OpA, A]
def put(k: String, v: Int): Op[Unit] = Free.liftF(Put(k, v))

val testInterp: OpA ~> Id = new (OpA ~> Id) { def apply[A](fa: OpA[A]) = ... }
program.foldMap(testInterp)
pitfalls: `Free` appears throughout the program's types: leaking it into every signature couples the code to the encoding; keep the algebra trait public and Free internal.
Stack safety depends on folding with `foldMap` into a suitable monad; hand-rolled recursion over `Free` loses the trampolining.
Diverging or unterminated programs are invisible in the type; add timeouts or step budgets at the runner.
